prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Near the dry river’s water-mark we found Your brother Minnegan, Flopped like a fish against the muddy ground. Beany, the kid whose yellow hair turns green, Told me to find you, even in the rain, And tell you he was drowned. I hid behind the chassis on the bank, The wreck of someone’s Ford: I was afraid to come and wake you drunk: You told me once the waking up was hard, The daylight beating at you like a board. Blood in my stomach sank. Beside, you told him never to go out Along the river-side Drinking and singing, clattering about. You might have thrown a rock at me and cried I was to blame, I let him fall in the road And pitch down on his side. Well, I’ll get hell enough when I get home For coming up this far, Leaving the note, and running as I came. I’ll go and tell my father where you are. You’d better go find Minnegan before Policemen hear and come. Beany went home, and I got sick and ran, You old son of a bitch. You better hurry down to Minnegan; He’s drunk or dying now, I don’t know which, Rolled in the roots and garbage like a fish, The poor old man.

outputs.L2:
Here's a rewritten version preserving the narrative content:

---

We discovered your brother Minnegan sprawled at the edge of the parched riverbed, thrown against the muck like a stranded fish. Beany—that boy whose blond hair takes on a greenish tint—sent me to track you down, rain or no rain, to break the news that he had drowned.

I crouched behind an abandoned Ford's frame on the bank, too scared to disturb your sleep since you'd been drinking. You once confessed that waking was brutal for you, with sunlight hammering at you like a plank. My gut twisted with dread.

Remember, you'd warned him repeatedly against wandering near that river, drinking and making noise. Perhaps you'll hurl a stone at me now, blaming me for letting him stumble and collapse on the roadside.

I know I'm in for punishment once I return home—having ventured this far, having left only a note, having fled the way I did. I intend to tell my father your whereabouts. You should locate Minnegan quickly, before the police catch wind of this.

Beany headed home. I felt nauseous and bolted, you miserable drunk. Get down to Minnegan fast—he's either intoxicated or fading, I can't say which, tangled among the roots and refuse like some discarded fish, that poor old soul.
outputs.L3:
I found him down by the dry riverbed, lying there flopped over like a fish somebody had thrown back too late—Minnegan, still and strange in a way I'd never seen a person be still before. The riverbed hadn't seen water in weeks, but he looked drowned all the same, like the ghost of some old flood had come back just for him and pulled him under one last time.

Beany was the one who sent me out into the rain to find you. She didn't say much, just pointed toward the door and told me to go, to run if I had to, and tell you what had happened to Minnegan before it was too late for whatever it was still worth. So I went, soaked through before I'd gone a block, my shoes filling up with water that didn't feel any different from the rain falling on my head.

When I got close to where you were, I stopped behind that old wrecked car—the one that's been sitting there so long the weeds have started growing up through the engine—and I crouched down low, hiding, not wanting to be the one to wake you. I knew what it did to you, coming up out of a drunk sleep too fast. I'd seen it before, the way your hands would shake and your eyes would look at me like I was something out of a bad dream. I didn't want to be that thing again. So I stayed there, wet and shivering, working up the nerve, thinking about how you'd told Minnegan more than once not to go down to the river drinking and singing the way he did, how you'd warned him that the water was low and the rocks were sharp and that nobody was going to come running if he got himself in trouble out there. He hadn't listened. Now here I was, the one who had to say so.

I knew, too, that I'd be in for it myself once I finally made it home—Father wasn't going to let it slide, me being gone so long, wandering so far in weather like this. But I'd already decided what I'd tell him: that I knew where you were, that I'd take him to you myself if he asked. Because more than anything, I needed you to get up, to shake off whatever sleep still had hold of you, and get down to that riverbed before the police did. I didn't want strangers finding Minnegan first. I wanted it to be you.
outputs.L4:
# The Messenger's Burden

I found him by the riverbed where the water used to run,
Face down in the cracked mud, still as the setting sun.
Minnegan—I called his name, though I knew he couldn't hear,
His breath had left him somewhere between the dust and fear.

I ran here quick as my legs could carry, but now I stand and wait,
Afraid to wake you from your sleep, afraid to seal his fate
By speaking words that tumble out and shatter this thin peace—
You always rage when woken rough, when dreams are forced to cease.

The whiskey's still upon your breath, I smell it from the door,
And I have seen what waking brings, I've seen it all before.
Your hands don't know their gentleness when sleep is torn away,
Your voice becomes a different thing, dark words you'd never say

If you were only sober now, if morning light were kind—
But morning waits for no one, sir, and neither does the mind
Of law that soon will come this way, with questions, with their eyes
That judge a father's failing by a brother's early demise.

I'm frightened of your anger, sir, I'm frightened of your grief,
But more I fear what happens if we're found without belief
That we tried to save him first, before the sheriff's car
Comes rolling up our gravel drive to see how far, how far

This family has fallen since the bottle took its hold.
Please, wake up now and listen—I am young but I've been told
That silence makes us guilty of the things we could have stopped.
Minnegan is lying there. The water's almost dropped

To nothing in that riverbed, like something dried to bone.
I cannot lift him by myself, I cannot go alone
Back to where he's fallen, back to where the current died—
I need you, drunk or angry, standing sober by my side.

So wake, please wake, before they come with sirens and with light,
Before the neighbors gather round to witness this sad sight.
Let's go together, find him now, while there's still time to know
If breath remains within his chest, if we can save him so.

I know you'll curse my waking you, I know you'll raise your hand,
But Minnegan is out there still, upon that barren land,
And every moment that we wait is time we cannot buy—
Please, father, rise and come with me, before we hear him die.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a narrative poem about a young speaker confessing to a drunk father figure that his brother Minnegan may have drowned in a river, using stark, working-class imagery?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Telling**

I found him where the porch light couldn't reach,
a bottle sweating rings into the wood,
his shirt gone loose, his knuckles thick and scarred
from twenty years of shift work at the mill.
I stood there like a fence post in the yard.

"Pa," I said, and something in my voice
made him look up the way a dog looks up
when it hears thunder that ain't thunder yet.

The river's been up high since Tuesday's rain,
brown as coffee, running fast and mean
past the old grain elevator, past
the rusted-out sedans along the bank
where Minnegan and I would go to fish,
to skip the flat stones, to forget the house.

"Pa, I got to tell you something now."
The words sat in my mouth like river stone,
too big to swallow, and too hard to spit.

He set the bottle down. I watched his hand—
that hand that built our porch, that hand that hit
me twice last winter when the money ran
clean out before the month did—watched it shake.

"Minnegan went in after that dog.
The Hendricks' dog, the one that's always loose.
It went in first. He went in after it.
I saw him go. I saw the water take
the both of them around the bend, past where
the willows drag their branches like they're tired,
past where the current pulls down toward the dam."

The moths were beating on the yellow bulb
like they were trying to get somewhere else.
My father's face went the color of ash,
went the color of the sky before snow,
went the color of a man who's lost
the only thing that made the mill worth it,
the only thing that made the whiskey wait
until after supper instead of before.

"He might have made it to the Simmons' bridge,"
I said, though I believed it like a prayer
you say because the silence is too big.
"I ran for help. I ran the whole way back.
They got the county boats out. They got lights."

He stood up slow, the way old buildings fall—
not all at once, but piece by piece, the way
a chimney leans before it finds the ground.
He didn't cry. Men like my father don't.
He just walked past me toward the pickup truck,
his boots against the gravel like a drum,
like something being buried, like a bell
they ring downtown when there's a fire to fight.

I stood there in the dark and let him go.
The river doesn't care whose son it takes.
It just keeps moving south, the way it always has,
past the mill, past the bridge, past everything
we ever tried to build to keep us safe.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem in the voice of a boy named Beany's friend, describing finding a body by a dried-up river and having to break the news, ending with a harsh curse at an old man.
counterfactuals.output:
**What We Found at Miller's Bend**

Beany saw it first,
that pale shape snagged
in the cracked mud
where the river used to run,
before the summer ate it whole.

He didn't say nothing.
Just stood there
like his boots grew roots,
finger pointing
same as a compass needle
finds north whether you want it to or not.

I made myself look.

A boot. Then a hand,
fingers curled like they were
still reaching for something
that got away downstream
years before the water did.

We didn't touch him.
Beany said don't,
like he'd read it in a book somewhere,
though I think he just knew
the way you know
not to put your hand on a stove twice.

We ran the whole way back,
lungs burning worse than August,
past the Hendersons' fence,
past the dog that always barks
but didn't that day—
even he knew something.

Momma's face when we told her.
That's the part I don't forget.
How she went the color of the riverbed,
grey and cracked,
like she was drying up too,
right there in the kitchen
with the bread half-kneaded on the counter.

She called the sheriff.
Beany sat on the porch step
and didn't cry
until later, alone,
when he thought nobody was looking.
I looked anyway.

By evening the whole town knew.
By evening old man Tucker
was sitting on his stoop
same as always,
spitting his tobacco in the dust,
saying *boys shouldn't play by dead rivers,
shouldn't go looking for trouble.*

Like we went looking.
Like the dead man climbed
out of the cracked earth
just to spite us,
just to ruin our whole summer
with his curled-up hand
and his boot full of nothing.

Like it was our fault
the water left
and something worse moved in.

You rotten old bastard,
you don't know a damn thing
about what we carry home with us
in the dark,
long after the water's gone
and the questions never dry up at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a dark, gritty poem featuring characters named Minnegan and Beany, a wrecked Ford by a riverbank, and a confession about running home scared—can you write it?
counterfactuals.output:
# What the River Kept

Minnegan found the Ford first, half-swallowed
in the mudbank, its grille grinning like a busted jaw,
windshield spidered white where something hit it once—
hard, and didn't stop to check.

Beany wouldn't go near it.
Stood back with his hands in his pockets,
kicking stones into the brown water,
saying *that thing's been dead longer than we've been alive.*

But Minnegan climbed in anyway,
sat behind a wheel gone green with rot,
pretended to drive somewhere else,
somewhere that wasn't this town,
this river, this rust-eaten hour.

*You remember,* Beany said, low,
*that night in October—*
Minnegan's hands went still on the wheel.

*I remember you crying,* Minnegan said.
*I remember you didn't.*

The confession came out sideways, the way truth does
when it's been buried too long in a chest:
*I ran,* Beany said. *When we heard it in the woods—
whatever it was—I ran home
and left you there in the dark.
I told everyone we got separated.
I told myself the same damn thing
for three years.*

The river didn't stop moving.
It never does, indifferent
to men and their small, rotting sins.

Minnegan looked at the cracked dashboard,
at the seat springs pushing through like ribs,
and said nothing for a long time—
long enough that Beany thought
this might be where it ends,
two men and a dead car
and a friendship gone to rust.

*I know,* Minnegan finally said.
*I heard you running.
I heard your feet on the leaves
and I thought—good.
At least one of us gets out.*

The Ford sat between them,
a monument to some other wreck—
older, quieter, the kind that happens
in the space between two people
where the truth should've gone
and didn't.

Beany sat down on the bumper,
rust flaking like dead skin,
and for once, neither of them
moved to leave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem that mimics the tone of mid-20th-century American poets like James Wright, focusing on poverty, drinking, death by a river, and a fractured family relationship.
counterfactuals.output:
**Below the Coal Tipple, Late October**

My father drank the color out of evenings,
sitting on the porch rail like a man
waiting for a train that stopped running
before I was born.

Downriver, the Ohio moved brown and patient,
carrying whatever the mills let go—
rust, and the small bones of fish,
and once, I heard, a man
who walked in wearing his good coat
because he had nowhere else to be beautiful.

I do not know if my father loved me.
He never said. He only pointed
at the barges some nights, said *look*,
as if the word itself were a kind of tenderness
he couldn't spend any other way.

We buried him in spring, which seemed wrong—
the dogwoods insisting on their white noise
while the ground opened like a mouth
that had said everything it was going to say.

I walked down after, alone,
past the shut-down depot, the weeds
coming up through the ties like green intentions.
The river didn't stop for him
any more than it stopped for the others,
the ones who went in quiet
some November, boots left folded
neat as a letter on the bank.

I stood there a long time, not praying,
just watching the water do the only thing
it knows how—
keep moving, keep taking
whatever the land can't hold anymore,
and mine, and mine, and mine.
